units.name: Exploring Data

concepts.intro: Every distribution of quantitative data is described by its shape (symmetric, skewed, unimodal/bimodal), center (mean or median), and spread (range, IQR, or standard deviation), along with any outliers.
b: Always describe distributions with SOCS: Shape, Outliers, Center, Spread, in context
Skewed left: tail points left, mean < median; skewed right: tail points right, mean > median
Symmetric distributions have mean ≈ median
Unimodal = one peak, bimodal = two peaks, uniform = flat
Use the shape to decide which center/spread measures are appropriate

concepts.intro: The mean is the arithmetic average and is sensitive to outliers/skew, while the median is the middle value and resists extreme values.
b: Mean: x̄ = (Σx)/n
Median: middle value of ordered data (average of two middle values if n is even)
Mean is pulled toward the tail in a skewed distribution; median is resistant
For skewed data or data with outliers, report the median as the 'typical' value
Mode is the most frequent value; useful mainly for categorical or discrete data

concepts.intro: Spread describes how variable the data are; range and IQR are resistant-friendly, while variance and standard deviation use every value.
b: Range = max − min
IQR = Q3 − Q1 (spread of the middle 50%), resistant to outliers
Variance: s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1); Standard deviation s = √(variance)
SD measures the typical distance of a value from the mean
Standard deviation is not resistant — outliers inflate it
Use IQR with median (skewed data); use SD with mean (roughly symmetric data)

concepts.intro: The five-number summary (min, Q1, median, Q3, max) is displayed visually with a boxplot, and the 1.5×IQR rule flags potential outliers.
b: Five-number summary: Min, Q1, Median, Q3, Max
Outlier rule: any value below Q1 − 1.5(IQR) or above Q3 + 1.5(IQR)
Boxplots show the IQR as a box with whiskers to the most extreme non-outlier values
Modified boxplots plot outliers as separate points
Boxplots are good for comparing distributions across groups side by side

concepts.intro: A z-score converts a raw value into the number of standard deviations it lies from the mean, letting you compare values from different distributions.
b: z = (x − μ) / σ (or (x − x̄)/s for sample data)
Positive z: value is above the mean; negative z: value is below the mean
Standardizing does not change the shape of a distribution
z-scores allow comparison of values measured on different scales (e.g., test scores from different exams)
Adding a constant to every value shifts center but not spread; multiplying by a constant changes both center and spread proportionally

concepts.intro: When comparing two or more distributions, always compare shape, center, spread, and outliers in context rather than describing them separately.
b: Use parallel boxplots, back-to-back stemplots, or dotplots to compare groups
Comment on which group has the higher center and which has more/less variability
Relative frequency (percent) is used, not counts, when group sizes differ
Density curves show the proportion of data as area under the curve, total area = 1
Always write comparative statements in context, using words like 'greater than' or 'less variable than'

keyFacts: IQR = Q3 − Q1; outliers lie beyond Q1 − 1.5·IQR or Q3 + 1.5·IQR
z = (x − μ)/σ
Mean is pulled toward the tail in skewed data; median resists skew
traps: ‘Skewed left’ describes the direction of the longer tail, not where most data pile up
Standard deviation can never be negative; a computed negative SD means an arithmetic error
Adding a constant to all data shifts the mean but leaves the standard deviation unchanged — only multiplying changes spread
Comparing distributions requires comparative language in context, not two separate one-group descriptions

units.name: Modeling Distributions

concepts.intro: A density curve is a smooth curve that models the shape of a distribution, where the total area underneath equals 1 and area corresponds to proportion of data.
b: Total area under a density curve = 1 (100% of data)
Area under the curve over an interval = proportion of observations in that interval
The median divides the area in half; the mean is the balance point of the curve
In a skewed density curve, the mean is pulled toward the longer tail relative to the median
Density curves are idealized models, not the actual data

concepts.intro: The Normal distribution is a symmetric, bell-shaped density curve fully described by its mean μ and standard deviation σ, following the Empirical (68-95-99.7) Rule.
b: Notation: N(μ, σ)
68% of values fall within 1 SD of the mean (μ ± σ)
95% of values fall within 2 SD of the mean (μ ± 2σ)
99.7% of values fall within 3 SD of the mean (μ ± 3σ)
Normal curves are symmetric with mean = median = mode at the center
Inflection points of the curve occur at μ ± σ

concepts.intro: Any Normal distribution can be converted to the standard Normal distribution N(0,1) by standardizing values with z = (x − μ)/σ.
b: z = (x − μ)/σ converts x to a standard score
Standard Normal distribution: N(0, 1)
Use a z-table or calculator (normalcdf) to find proportions/probabilities
invNorm is used to find a value given a percentile/proportion
z-scores let you compare observations from different Normal distributions

concepts.intro: Calculator functions normalcdf and invNorm let you compute probabilities/proportions and find values from percentiles for any Normal distribution.
b: normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) finds the proportion/probability between two values
invNorm(percentile, μ, σ) finds the value at a given percentile
For 'less than', use normalcdf(-1E99, x, μ, σ); for 'greater than', use normalcdf(x, 1E99, μ, σ)
Always sketch and shade the Normal curve before calculating
Check reasonableness: answers should be between 0 and 1 for probabilities

concepts.intro: A Normal probability plot (or comparing the data to the 68-95-99.7 rule) helps determine whether a data set is approximately Normally distributed.
b: A Normal probability plot that is roughly linear suggests the data are approximately Normal
Curvature in the plot indicates skewness or non-Normality
Compare observed percentages within 1, 2, 3 SD of the mean to 68%, 95%, 99.7%
Histograms/boxplots showing strong skew or outliers suggest data are not Normal
Many statistical procedures assume Normality, so checking it matters for inference later

keyFacts: Empirical Rule: 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ of μ
z = (x − μ)/σ ; x = μ + zσ
Total area under any density curve = 1
Standard Normal: N(0,1)
traps: The Empirical Rule only applies to (approximately) Normal distributions, not all distributions
A Normal probability plot with a clear curve — not a straight line — signals the data are NOT Normal
Area under a density curve represents proportion, not probability of a single exact point (P(X = x) = 0 for continuous variables)
z-scores can be negative; a negative z simply means the value is below the mean, not an error

units.name: Describing Bivariate Data

concepts.intro: A scatterplot displays the relationship between two quantitative variables, revealing direction, form, strength, and unusual features (outliers).
b: Explanatory variable (x) is plotted on the horizontal axis; response variable (y) on the vertical axis
Direction: positive (as x increases, y increases) or negative association
Form: linear or nonlinear (curved) pattern
Strength: how closely points follow the pattern (tight vs. scattered)
Always note any outliers or unusual points separately

concepts.intro: The correlation coefficient r measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables, ranging from -1 to 1.
b: r ranges from -1 to +1; sign matches the direction of association
r close to ±1 indicates a strong linear relationship; r close to 0 indicates a weak/no linear relationship
r measures only linear association — it can be misleading for curved relationships
r has no units and is not affected by which variable is x or y
r is strongly affected by outliers
r² (coefficient of determination) is discussed separately

concepts.intro: The least-squares regression line ŷ = a + bx minimizes the sum of squared residuals and is used to predict y from x.
b: Slope b = r(sy/sx); the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
Interpretation of slope: 'for each one-unit increase in x, ŷ is predicted to change by b units'
Interpretation of y-intercept a: predicted value of y when x = 0 (only meaningful if x=0 is in scope)
Extrapolation (predicting far outside the observed x-range) is unreliable
Regression line is only appropriate for genuinely linear relationships

concepts.intro: A residual is the difference between an observed and predicted value (residual = y − ŷ), and residual plots help check whether a linear model is appropriate.
b: Residual = observed y − predicted ŷ
A residual plot with no pattern (random scatter around 0) supports a linear model
A curved pattern in the residual plot indicates the relationship is not linear
Increasing spread (fan shape) in residuals indicates non-constant variability
The sum of residuals for a least-squares line is always 0

concepts.intro: r² is the proportion of variation in y that is explained by the linear regression on x, and is always between 0 and 1.
b: r² = (correlation r)²
Interpretation: 'r²×100% of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x'
r² closer to 1 means the regression line explains most of the variability in y
r² does not indicate causation, only explanatory strength of the linear model
Standard deviation of residuals (s) measures typical prediction error in y's units

concepts.intro: Outliers and especially influential points (often high-leverage x-values) can dramatically change the regression line, and nonlinear data may require transformation.
b: An outlier in regression has a large residual (far from the pattern)
An influential point substantially changes the slope/intercept if removed, often due to extreme x-value
Log or power transformations can linearize exponential or power-model data before regression
Always check a residual plot before trusting a linear model's predictions
Correlation/regression describe association, never prove causation

keyFacts: b = r(sy/sx); line passes through (x̄, ȳ)
r² = r²; proportion of variation in y explained by x
residual = y − ŷ; residuals sum to 0 for LSRL
-1 ≤ r ≤ 1; r measures strength/direction of LINEAR association only
traps: Correlation does NOT imply causation — a strong r only shows association
A high r² does not fix a nonlinear relationship; always check the residual plot first
Extrapolation beyond the observed x-range is unreliable even with a high r²
Correlation r is not resistant — a single outlier can drastically change its value

quiz.q: A distribution has mean 50 and median 60 with a long tail to the left. This distribution is best described as:
quiz.e: Mean less than median with a long left tail indicates left skew.

quiz.q: Which measure of center is resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: The median only depends on the middle value(s), so extreme values don't affect it much.

quiz.q: A data set: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Find the mean.
For the data set 2, 4, 4, 6, 9, what is the median?
quiz.e: Ordered data's middle value (3rd of 5) is 4.

quiz.q: If a distribution is strongly skewed right, which measure of center is more appropriate to report?
quiz.e: Median resists the pull of the long right tail and reflects the typical value.

quiz.q: The IQR of a data set is the difference between:
quiz.e: IQR = Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of data.

quiz.q: A value is an outlier by the 1.5×IQR rule if it is:
quiz.e: The 1.5×IQR rule flags values more than 1.5 IQRs below Q1 or above Q3.

quiz.q: Data set has Q1 = 10, Q3 = 22. What is the upper fence for outliers?
Which of the following is NOT resistant to outliers?
quiz.e: Standard deviation uses every value including extreme ones, so it is not resistant.

quiz.q: A test score of 82 has a z-score of 1.5 when μ = 70 and σ = 8. Is this consistent?
quiz.e: (82-70)/8 = 12/8 = 1.5, so the z-score is correct.

quiz.q: A z-score tells you:
o: How many standard deviations a value is from the mean
quiz.e: z-scores measure distance from the mean in standard deviation units.

quiz.q: If every value in a data set is multiplied by 3, what happens to the standard deviation?
quiz.e: Multiplying data by a constant multiplies the SD by the absolute value of that constant.

quiz.q: If a constant of 5 is added to every data value, the standard deviation:
quiz.e: Adding a constant shifts every value equally, changing the mean/median but not the spread.

quiz.q: A boxplot's box represents:
quiz.e: The box spans from Q1 to Q3, capturing the middle 50% of the data.

quiz.q: In a boxplot, whiskers extend to:
o: The most extreme values that are not outliers
Exactly 1.5 IQR from the box always
quiz.e: Whiskers reach the most extreme data points within the fences (non-outliers).

quiz.q: When comparing two groups' distributions, you should:
o: Describe each group separately with no comparison
Use comparative language like 'greater than' in context
quiz.e: AP scoring requires explicit comparative statements in context, e.g., 'Group A has a higher median than Group B.'

quiz.q: A distribution is symmetric and unimodal. Which relationship best fits?
quiz.e: In symmetric distributions, mean and median are approximately equal.

quiz.q: Which plot is best for comparing the shapes of two large data sets side-by-side?
quiz.e: Parallel boxplots or back-to-back stemplots allow visual comparison of shape, center, and spread.

quiz.q: The variance is defined as:
quiz.e: Sample variance s² = Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1).

quiz.q: Standard deviation is the square root of:
quiz.e: By definition, s = √(s²), the square root of variance.

quiz.q: A data set has an SD of 0. What does this tell you?
quiz.e: SD = 0 only if there is no variability, meaning every value equals the mean.

quiz.q: Which of the following would most increase the standard deviation of a data set?
o: Adding a value far from the mean
Adding a value equal to the mean
quiz.e: Adding a value far from the mean increases the squared deviations, raising SD.

quiz.q: For a right-skewed distribution, which is typically true?
quiz.e: In right skew, the long right tail pulls the mean above the median.

quiz.q: A frequency table shows 10 students scored 60-69, 15 scored 70-79, 5 scored 80-89. This is an example of:
quiz.e: Grouping values into intervals with counts is grouped/binned frequency data.

quiz.q: Which statistic uses only two of the five-number summary values?
quiz.e: IQR = Q3 − Q1, using only two of the five-number summary's values.

quiz.q: A percentile of 90 means:
o: 90% of values are above this value
90% of values are at or below this value
The value is 90 units above the mean
quiz.e: The pth percentile is the value below which p% of the data fall.

quiz.q: Which is more affected by an extreme outlier: mean or median?
quiz.e: The mean incorporates every value directly into its sum, so a single extreme value shifts it substantially.

quiz.q: A cumulative relative frequency graph (ogive) is used to find:
quiz.e: Ogives plot cumulative percentages, letting you read off percentiles and the median.

quiz.q: If a distribution is uniform, its shape is:
o: Flat, roughly equal frequency across values
quiz.e: Uniform distributions have roughly constant frequency/density across the range.

quiz.q: A stemplot splitting stems by 'leaves 0-4' and 'leaves 5-9' is called:
quiz.e: A split stemplot divides each stem into two lines to show more detail in the shape.

quiz.q: A set of data has mean 20 and SD 4. Convert x = 28 to a z-score.
With mean 100 and SD 15 (like IQ scores), what raw score corresponds to z = -1?
Which graphical display is most appropriate for a single quantitative variable's shape?
quiz.e: Histograms display the distribution shape of quantitative data using bins.

quiz.q: A pie chart is appropriate for:
o: Categorical data showing parts of a whole
quiz.e: Pie charts represent proportions of categories, not quantitative distributions.

quiz.q: Which is true about the sum of deviations from the mean, Σ(x − x̄)?
quiz.e: By definition, deviations from the mean sum to zero, which is why squared deviations are used for variance.

quiz.q: A class's exam scores are heavily skewed left with several low outliers. The best summary uses:
quiz.e: Median and IQR are resistant to skew and outliers, making them appropriate here.

quiz.q: Which change to a data set would NOT affect the IQR?
o: Adding a constant to every value
Multiplying every value by a constant
quiz.e: Adding a constant shifts all values equally, so Q3 − Q1 (IQR) is unchanged.

quiz.q: Two data sets have the same mean but different standard deviations. What does the larger SD indicate?
quiz.e: A larger SD indicates data points are more spread out from the mean on average.

quiz.q: A z-score of -2.5 for a value means:
o: The value is 2.5 units above the mean
The value is 2.5 standard deviations below the mean
quiz.e: Negative z-scores indicate the value lies below the mean, here by 2.5 SDs.

quiz.q: When describing shape, 'bimodal' means the distribution has:
quiz.e: Bimodal distributions show two distinct peaks, often suggesting two underlying groups.

quiz.q: A Normal distribution has μ = 100, σ = 15. What percent of values fall between 85 and 115?
quiz.e: 85 and 115 are μ ± 1σ, capturing 68% by the Empirical Rule.

quiz.q: For N(100, 15), what range captures 95% of values?
quiz.e: 95% falls within μ ± 2σ = 100 ± 30, i.e., 70 to 130.

quiz.q: What is the z-score for x = 130 in N(100, 15)?
In a standard Normal distribution, what is P(Z < 0)?
quiz.e: The standard Normal is symmetric about 0, so exactly half the area lies below 0.

quiz.q: Total area under any density curve equals:
quiz.e: By definition, the total area under a density curve is always 1 (100%).

quiz.q: Which best describes the Normal distribution's shape?
quiz.e: The Normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, centered at μ.

quiz.q: For N(50, 10), what is the value at the 84th percentile (approximately)?
quiz.e: 84th percentile ≈ μ + 1σ (since 50% + 34% ≈ 84%), so 50+10 = 60.

quiz.q: A student scores z = -1.5 on an exam that is N(75, 8). What is their raw score?
Which calculator function finds the proportion of area between two z-values?
quiz.e: normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) computes the area (proportion) between two values.

quiz.q: Which calculator function finds a value given a percentile?
quiz.e: invNorm(area, μ, σ) returns the x-value corresponding to a given cumulative proportion.

quiz.q: A Normal probability plot that curves noticeably suggests:
o: The sample size is too large
quiz.e: Systematic curvature in a Normal probability plot indicates departure from Normality.

quiz.q: What proportion of a Normal distribution lies more than 2 SD from the mean?
quiz.e: Since 95% lies within 2 SD, the remaining 5% lies beyond ±2σ (both tails combined).

quiz.q: For a standard Normal variable, P(Z > 1.96) is approximately:
quiz.e: About 2.5% of the area lies in each tail beyond ±1.96 in the standard Normal (from the 95% rule).

quiz.q: A data set's middle 68% closely matches ±1 SD from the mean, and a Normal probability plot is roughly linear. This suggests:
quiz.e: Both pieces of evidence — matching Empirical Rule percentages and a linear probability plot — support approximate Normality.

quiz.q: If X ~ N(20, 5), what is P(X < 20)?
quiz.e: 20 is the mean, and Normal distributions are symmetric, so exactly half the area lies below the mean.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a property of the Normal distribution?
quiz.e: The Normal distribution extends from -∞ to +∞; it is not bounded between 0 and 1 (that describes probability values, not x-values).

quiz.q: For N(0,1), invNorm(0.5) equals:
quiz.e: The median (50th percentile) of the standard Normal distribution is 0.

quiz.q: A z-score of 0 means the value is:
quiz.e: z = 0 occurs only when x = μ, since z = (x−μ)/σ.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to compute P(X > 85) for N(80, 6)?
quiz.e: 'Greater than 85' uses the upper tail: normalcdf from 85 to infinity.

quiz.q: A distribution's Normal probability plot is a straight, roughly 45° line. This indicates:
o: Good fit to a Normal model
quiz.e: A linear Normal probability plot indicates the data closely follow a Normal distribution.

quiz.q: What is the interquartile range of the standard Normal distribution, approximately?
quiz.e: Q1 ≈ -0.675 and Q3 ≈ 0.675 for N(0,1), giving IQR ≈ 1.35.

quiz.q: Heights of adult men are approximately N(70, 3) inches. What percent are taller than 76 inches?
quiz.e: 76 is 2 SD above the mean (70+2×3); about 2.5% of a Normal distribution lies beyond +2σ in one tail.

quiz.q: Which value is closer to the mean in a right-skewed distribution: the mean or the median?
quiz.e: In skewed distributions, the median is less affected by the tail and stays closer to the bulk of the data than the mean.

quiz.q: For X ~ N(60, 8), find the z-score for x = 44.
Approximately what percent of a Normal distribution lies between the mean and 1 SD above it?
quiz.e: Half of the 68% within ±1σ lies on each side, so about 34% lies between the mean and +1σ.

quiz.q: A calculator gives invNorm(0.90, 100, 15) = 119.2. This means:
quiz.e: invNorm returns the value below which the given proportion (90%) of the distribution lies.

quiz.q: Which scenario is LEAST likely to be well-modeled by a Normal distribution?
o: Measurement errors in a precise instrument
quiz.e: Income distributions are typically strongly right-skewed, not Normal.

quiz.q: If a distribution is exactly Normal, what is true of skewness?
quiz.e: Normal distributions are perfectly symmetric, so skewness is zero.

quiz.q: The 'inflection points' of a Normal curve occur at:
quiz.e: The curve changes concavity (inflection) exactly one standard deviation from the mean on each side.

quiz.q: A test is Normally distributed with mean 500 and SD 100. What score is at the 97.5th percentile (approx)?
quiz.e: 97.5th percentile ≈ μ + 2σ (since 95% is within ±2σ, leaving 2.5% above), so 500+200 = 700.

quiz.q: Which is true about comparing z-scores from two different Normal distributions?
o: A higher z-score always means a higher raw score in both distributions and standardized comparisons are valid
Only means can be compared, not z-scores
quiz.e: Standardizing puts values on a common scale, so z-scores can be validly compared across different Normal distributions.

quiz.q: Which best describes 'proportion of area under a density curve between a and b'?
o: The count of values between a and b
The proportion of observations between a and b
The mean of values between a and b
The SD between a and b
quiz.e: Area under a density curve directly represents the proportion of the distribution in that interval.

quiz.q: For a Normal distribution, which measure of center and spread fully determine the curve?
quiz.e: A Normal distribution N(μ, σ) is completely specified by its mean and standard deviation.

quiz.q: What is P(Z < -1.5) for the standard Normal distribution, approximately?
quiz.e: Using the standard Normal table, P(Z < -1.5) ≈ 0.0668, closest to 0.07.

quiz.q: Test scores are N(70, 10). A score of 90 is how many standard deviations above the mean?
Which statement about the median of a Normal distribution is true?
o: It is always less than the mean
It is always greater than the mean
quiz.e: Because the Normal distribution is symmetric, mean = median = mode.

quiz.q: Which is the best tool to formally assess Normality using calculator/software output?
quiz.e: The Normal probability plot is specifically designed to assess how well data fit a Normal model.

quiz.q: A Normal distribution has σ = 0. What does this imply?
o: Impossible for real data; SD must be positive
All values equal the mean exactly
quiz.e: An SD of 0 would mean zero variability — every value equal to the mean — which real continuous Normal data cannot have (σ > 0 by definition of the model).

quiz.q: Which pair of z-scores captures the middle 95% of a standard Normal distribution most precisely?
quiz.e: The precise z-value for 95% (2.5% in each tail) is ±1.96, though ±2 is the Empirical Rule approximation.

quiz.q: A company's part diameters are N(2.00, 0.01) cm. What proportion of parts are between 1.98 and 2.02 cm?
quiz.e: 1.98 and 2.02 are μ ± 2σ, capturing about 95% by the Empirical Rule.

quiz.q: A scatterplot shows points closely following an upward line. This suggests:
quiz.e: Points trending upward tightly indicate a strong positive linear correlation.

quiz.q: Correlation r = -0.92 indicates:
quiz.e: r close to -1 indicates a strong negative linear relationship.

quiz.q: Which value of r indicates the weakest linear relationship?
quiz.e: r close to 0 indicates little to no linear relationship.

quiz.q: If the regression line is ŷ = 5 + 2x, the slope means:
o: y increases by 5 for each unit increase in x
y increases by 2 for each unit increase in x
x increases by 2 for each unit increase in y
The line passes through the origin
quiz.e: The slope (2) represents the predicted change in y per one-unit increase in x.

quiz.q: Given b = 3, sx = 2, sy = 6, find r.
If r = 0.8, what is r² and its interpretation?
o: 0.64; 64% of variation in y explained by x
0.8; 80% of variation in y explained by x
quiz.e: r² = 0.8² = 0.64, meaning 64% of the variation in y is explained by the linear relationship with x.

quiz.q: A residual is calculated as:
quiz.e: Residual = observed y minus predicted ŷ.

quiz.q: A residual plot shows a clear curved (U-shaped) pattern. This suggests:
o: The linear model is NOT appropriate; relationship may be nonlinear
quiz.e: A curved residual pattern indicates the data have a nonlinear relationship not captured by the line.

quiz.q: An influential point in regression is one that:
o: Substantially changes the regression line if removed
Is always the point with the largest y-value
quiz.e: Influential points, often with extreme x-values, significantly alter the slope/intercept when removed.

quiz.q: The sum of the residuals for a least-squares regression line is always:
quiz.e: By the least-squares property, positive and negative residuals cancel exactly to zero.

quiz.q: Which of these does correlation NOT measure?
quiz.e: Correlation measures association, never causation.

quiz.q: A least-squares regression line always passes through:
quiz.e: The LSRL always passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ).

quiz.q: If x and y have correlation r = 0.6, then y and x (switching axes) have correlation:
quiz.e: Correlation is symmetric — it does not depend on which variable is called x or y.

quiz.q: Extrapolation refers to:
o: Predicting y for x-values within the observed range
Predicting y for x-values far outside the observed range
quiz.e: Extrapolation is predicting outside the range of observed x-values, which is unreliable.

quiz.q: A study finds ice cream sales and drowning deaths are positively correlated. The best explanation is:
o: A lurking variable (hot weather) causes both to increase
The correlation is definitely due to chance
quiz.e: Both variables increase in summer due to a lurking (confounding) variable: warm weather.

quiz.q: Which transformation is commonly used to linearize exponential growth data before regression?
o: Taking the square root of x
quiz.e: For exponential relationships, plotting log(y) vs. x often linearizes the data.

quiz.q: A scatterplot's form is described as 'curved.' Which statistic is inappropriate to summarize this relationship?
quiz.e: Correlation r only quantifies linear association, so it's a poor summary for a clearly curved pattern.

quiz.q: If the standard deviation of residuals (s) is small, this suggests:
o: Poor predictions using the regression line
Good predictions; points are close to the line
The line has a negative slope
quiz.e: A small s means the observed values are, on average, close to their predicted values.

quiz.q: Given x̄ = 10, ȳ = 50, and slope b = 4, find the y-intercept a.
Using ŷ = 10 + 4x, predict y when x = 5.
Which best describes 'strength' in a scatterplot?
o: How closely points follow the pattern/form
Whether the slope is positive or negative
quiz.e: Strength refers to how tightly the points cluster around the trend (form).

quiz.q: A negative residual means:
o: The observed value is above the regression line
The observed value is below the regression line
quiz.e: A negative residual (y − ŷ < 0) means the actual value fell below the predicted value.

quiz.q: If r = 0, this means:
o: No relationship of any kind exists
No LINEAR relationship exists (there could still be a strong nonlinear one)
quiz.e: r=0 rules out linear association but does not rule out other (e.g., curved) relationships.

quiz.q: Which point would most likely be influential in a regression?
o: A point near x̄ with a small residual
A point with an extreme x-value far from the rest
A point exactly on the regression line
quiz.e: Points with extreme (high-leverage) x-values have the most potential to influence the slope.

quiz.q: What does the coefficient of determination NOT tell you?
o: The proportion of variation in y explained by x
Whether the relationship is linear (must check residual plot too)
How well the model fits compared to using ȳ alone
quiz.e: r² alone doesn't confirm linearity — you must examine the residual plot to check the linear model is appropriate.

quiz.q: Correlation is unitless because:
o: It is calculated using standardized (z-score) values
quiz.e: r is computed from the average product of standardized x and y values, removing units.

quiz.q: A regression's residual plot shows random scatter around zero with no pattern. This means:
o: The linear model is a poor fit
The linear model is a reasonable fit
quiz.e: Random, patternless residuals support that a linear model is appropriate for the data.

quiz.q: Which is true if two variables have a strong positive association but r is calculated as low (e.g., 0.1)?
o: The data must be normally distributed
quiz.e: A visually strong but non-linear association can still yield a low r, since r measures only linear strength.

quiz.q: Which measure describes the typical prediction error of a regression in the units of y?
quiz.e: s, the standard deviation of the residuals, estimates the typical size of prediction errors.

quiz.q: A scatterplot of weight (x) vs. height (y) shows a moderate positive linear trend with r=0.65. What is r²?
Doubling every x-value in a data set (with y unchanged) affects r how?
quiz.e: Correlation is invariant to linear transformations (scaling/shifting) of either variable.

quiz.q: A 'lurking variable' is:
o: A variable not measured that influences both the explanatory and response variables
Always the cause of the outcome
quiz.e: A lurking variable is unmeasured but affects the apparent relationship between the two studied variables.

quiz.q: Which of the following would make extrapolation especially risky?
o: Predicting for an x-value within the data range
Predicting for an x-value slightly outside the data range where the trend clearly continues
Predicting for an x-value far outside the observed range, where the relationship may change
Using the regression equation as given
quiz.e: Far outside the observed range, there's no evidence the same linear trend continues, making predictions unreliable.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a residual plot?
o: To assess whether a linear model is appropriate for the data
To find outliers in x only
quiz.e: Residual plots reveal patterns (curvature, changing spread) that indicate whether linear regression is suitable.

quiz.q: A regression of study hours (x) on test score (y) gives ŷ = 60 + 3x. Predict the score for 10 hours studied.
In the equation ŷ = 60 + 3x for study hours and test scores, the intercept 60 means:
o: The predicted score with 0 hours studied
quiz.e: The y-intercept is the predicted y-value when x = 0, here 0 hours of studying.

quiz.q: Which correlation value would produce the steepest positive regression slope, all else equal?
quiz.e: With sx and sy fixed, a larger positive r produces a steeper positive slope since b = r(sy/sx).

quiz.q: A scatterplot shows no visible pattern between x and y at all. The correlation r is likely:
quiz.e: No visible association suggests weak or no linear relationship, so r should be near 0.

quiz.q: Which is true about r² compared to r?
o: r² and r are always equal
r² has the same sign as the slope
quiz.e: Since r² is a squared value, it always falls between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%).

quiz.q: A residual plot shows increasing spread of points as x increases (a 'fan' shape). This indicates:
quiz.e: A fan-shaped residual plot shows that variability in y is not constant across x, violating a key regression assumption.
